prescriptions.rule: Typical early-refill ('refill too soon') edits: non-controlled refill allowed after 75% of days' supply used (day 23 of a 30-day fill, day 68 of a 90-day fill); controlled substances after 80% (day 24 / day 72).
prescriptions.note: From search summary of plan documents (HMSA, NC State Health Plan). Thresholds are set by each insurer/PBM, not by law; CMS Part D Benefits Manual ch. 6 treats early-refill edits as a utilization tool. Not read on a CMS page.

prescriptions.rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §4064.5: a pharmacist may dispense not more than a 90-day supply of a non-controlled dangerous drug where the prescription specifies a smaller initial quantity followed by refills, if the patient has completed an initial 30-day supply, total quantity does not exceed what was authorized, and the prescriber has not indicated otherwise; the prescriber must be notified.
prescriptions.note: Read on FindLaw (a third-party mirror of the statute), not on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.

prescriptions.rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §4063: no dangerous drug prescription may be refilled except on the prescriber's authorization; controlled substances may not be designated 'refill as needed'. Health & Safety Code §11166: no controlled-substance prescription filled more than six months after the date written.
prescriptions.note: From search summary of FindLaw/Justia statute text. No California statutory expiry for non-controlled prescriptions was found.

prescriptions.rule: NYSED Office of the Professions pharmacy FAQ: effective 2025-10-07 non-controlled prescriptions must be transferred in full including all refills; effective 2026-04-14 controlled-substance prescriptions may be transferred between pharmacies subject to PHL Article 33 and 10 NYCRR Part 80. Refill instructions may be a number of times, a time period such as one year, or 'prn'.
prescriptions.note: Transfer rules read on the NYSED page. The 'one year / prn' refill-instruction wording came from the search summary of the same site. Neither the FAQ nor 8 NYCRR Part 63 states a statutory expiry for non-controlled prescriptions.

prescriptions.rule: Schedule III and IV controlled substances may not be filled or refilled more than six months after the date written, nor refilled more than five times, unless renewed by the practitioner. Non-controlled prescriptions must state number of refills (or PRN / ad lib) under Conn. Gen. Stat. §20-614.
prescriptions.note: From search summary; Justia returned 403 and cga.ct.gov failed a certificate check. No one-year non-controlled expiry was found in CT law.

prescriptions.rule: NHS prescription charge per item; charge is per medicine item, not per prescription form. Free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
prescriptions.note: £9.90 per item read on nhs.uk. PPC prices read on Community Pharmacy England (https://cpe.org.uk/our-news/nhs-prescription-charges-frozen-for-the-second-year-running/), which reports the DHSC announcement — the national pharmacy-contractor body, not DHSC itself.

prescriptions.rule: An FP10 prescription is valid for 6 months from its date. Schedule 2, 3 and 4 controlled drugs: 28 days. Repeatable prescriptions: first dispensing within 6 months (28 days for Schedule 4 CDs); after first dispensing the repeats run as the prescription states.
prescriptions.note: NHS Business Services Authority's own FAQ. nhs.uk charges page also says most prescriptions last 6 months and controlled drugs 28 days.

prescriptions.rule: Repeat prescriptions are ordered from the GP surgery via the NHS App or NHS website, other online services/apps, or by contacting the surgery. Request up to 5 working days before you need the medicine.
prescriptions.note: Read on nhs.uk. GP practice pages (e.g. Prentis Medical Centre) say to allow two full working days for processing; that is per-practice, not national. The typical 28-day supply was not found on an NHS page.

prescriptions.rule: All prescriptions for prescription drugs remain valid unless otherwise specified by the prescriber; pharmacists must use judgement when much time has passed. Controlled substance prescriptions expire two years from the date the pharmacy receives them (or the date written, per Health Canada). Benzodiazepines/targeted substances: refill only if less than one year since issue.
prescriptions.note: Ontario College of Pharmacists' own fact sheet. The benzodiazepine one-year line came from the search summary of this page; the fetch itself reported the two-year controlled-substance rule.

prescriptions.rule: Ontario Drug Benefit pays for at most a 100-day supply per dispensing (since 2018-08-01); generally a maximum of 2 dispensing fees per 28 days for a listed drug.
prescriptions.note: 100-day maximum read on ontario.ca. The '2 fees per 28 days' rule came from the search summary of this page.

prescriptions.rule: ODB co-payment: up to $6.11 per prescription for most recipients; $2 for low-income seniors in the Seniors Co-Payment Program.
prescriptions.note: From search summary; not on the ontario.ca page fetched. The ministry's ODB dispensing fee to pharmacies, and private-pay dispensing fees, were not found on an official page.

prescriptions.rule: All prescriptions (new and existing) are valid for up to two years from the prescribing date, except benzodiazepines or other targeted substances, valid up to one year. Pharmacists may renew or adapt within the original expiry.
prescriptions.note: College of Pharmacists of BC's own page. A search summary also stated refills (except oral contraceptives) are valid for at most one year from the prescribing date; that was not confirmed on the page read.

prescriptions.rule: Maximum dispensing fee reimbursed by PharmaCare.
prescriptions.note: Read on gov.bc.ca (page last updated 2026-07-06). Search summary said the fee rose from $10 to $11 on 2026-01-02; that date was not read on the page. This is what PharmaCare reimburses, not what a cash-paying patient is charged.

prescriptions.rule: Drugs Payment Scheme: an individual or family pays no more than the monthly threshold for approved drugs, medicines and appliances.
prescriptions.note: HSE page says 'Apply for a Drugs Payment Scheme card if you pay more than €80 a month'. Citizens Information and third-party summaries give €80 as the 2026 cap. Irish Times (2026-09-23) reports a proposed policy that would raise patient contributions — watch Budget 2027.

prescriptions.rule: Medical card (GMS) prescription charge per item, with a monthly maximum; HSE refunds overpayment annually; a family certificate can be registered.

Acuerdo (DOF, signed 2010-05-17; in force 90 days after publication, 2010-08-25): antibiotics may be sold and dispensed 'única y exclusivamente contra la exhibición de la receta médica'. Each time it is filled the pharmacy stamps (sella) the prescription; when the prescribed quantity is exhausted the pharmacy retains it; retained prescriptions are kept 365 calendar days; the prescription may only be filled within the duration of the treatment. Topical, ophthalmic and nasal presentations were excluded from the COFEPRIS list.
prescriptions.note: Read on the Diario Oficial de la Federación (SIDOF) text. The effective date and excluded presentations are from Expansión (https://expansion.mx/economia/2010/08/04/cofepris-enlista-antibioticos-por-receta).

prescriptions.rule: Ley General de Salud Art. 226 classes: I special permit/prescription from Secretaría de Salud; II prescription retained by pharmacy, valid 30 days; III prescription may be filled up to three times, retained on the third; IV prescription refillable as many times as the doctor indicates; V no prescription, sold only in pharmacies; VI no prescription, may be sold outside pharmacies. Fractions V and VI are the over-the-counter classes.
prescriptions.note: Read on leyes-mx.com, a third-party copy of the law, not diputados.gob.mx. Which specific products are OTC (e.g. paracetamol, ibuprofen) was not listed.
